title: MCP-Persona: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Real-World Personal Applications via Environment Simulation
one_liner: Build a benchmark for agents that use personal apps and accounts, because real tool use breaks in ways that generic public-tool benchmarks do not capture.
lead: Many agent benchmarks focus on public information tools such as search, browsing, or generic APIs. Real personal tool use is harder. The agent must act through an individual account, respect personal state, interpret private histories, and recover from side effects that depend on that user's environment. MCP-Persona is a benchmark built for that setting. It simulates real personal applications and account-specific tools so researchers can measure where today's agents fail and why those failures appear.

problem.h2: Why public-tool benchmarks miss the hard part of personal tool use
paras: An agent that performs well on generic tools may still fail badly on personal applications such as social platforms, chat systems, or work suites. In those settings, success depends on user-specific state: prior messages, account permissions, private data, and local conventions.

Generic benchmarks remove much of that complexity. They often test information lookup or public workflows where the environment is largely the same for every run. The paper argues that this hides an important weakness because real assistants must act correctly inside personalized environments where the same instruction can require different steps for different accounts.

callout.html: Benchmark agents in simulated personal application environments, because evaluating account-specific tool use requires private state, permissions, and user history to be part of the task.

steps.text: Create tasks that require account-specific context so the benchmark reflects real assistant usage.
Provide application state, histories, permissions, and local data because those factors determine the correct action path.
Let agents call realistic personal tools so evaluation covers the same control pattern used in deployment settings.
Evaluate several strong agents on the same tasks so the benchmark can reveal current limits.
Record tool choice, state use, and completion outcomes because diagnosis is as important as the headline score.

paras: The paper changes agent evaluation from public generic tools to realistic personal application environments with account-specific state.
object.object: the benchmark environment used to test tool-using agents

hidden.name: environment personalization load
paras: The hidden quantity is how much account-specific context a task depends on. Some tasks require only one obvious tool call. Others require reading personal history, checking permissions, selecting the right account object, and avoiding destructive side effects.

MCP-Persona makes that load visible by simulating personal environments directly. This matters because an agent can appear strong on generic benchmarks while failing as soon as personal state becomes part of the decision process.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark tasks where success depends heavily on personal state and account-specific branching.

reads.html: This quantity asks how much the task depends on who the user is and what their environment currently contains. Personal tool use gets harder as that dependence rises because the correct path becomes more state-specific.
The benchmark targets personalized MCP tool use where agent decisions depend on private account state, local data, and application-specific workflow context.

mechanism.h2: Why this benchmark reveals failures that earlier ones miss
paras: A benchmark only tests what it includes. If the environment removes private state and personal branching, an agent never has to prove that it can reason about those factors. MCP-Persona includes them directly, so failures that would appear in deployment also appear during evaluation.

Environment simulation is important because personal applications cannot be benchmarked only by static text descriptions. The correct next step often depends on current account content and permissions. By simulating those details, the benchmark forces the agent to read state, choose tools accordingly, and recover when an early action was based on a wrong assumption.

This design produces stronger diagnosis because researchers can see whether failure came from missing state inspection, wrong tool selection, or poor handling of user-specific constraints. That is more actionable than a single task success number.

stages.s: benchmark records success and failure type

math.words: A simple summary is to reward successful task completion and subtract penalties for state misuse and failed recovery, because a personal-tool agent must do more than pick the right final tool once.
math.equation: benchmark_score = success_rate - alpha * state_errors - beta * recovery_failures
symbols: penalty weight on mistakes caused by ignoring or misreading user state
wrong actions caused by bad use of personal context
penalty weight on failure to recover after a wrong step
cases where the agent cannot repair the task after an early mistake

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Agent A finishes 8 of 10 tasks, so success_rate = 0.8.
It makes 1 state-related mistake and 2 failed recoveries.
If alpha = 0.1 and beta = 0.1, its score is 0.8 - 0.1 - 0.2 = 0.5.
Agent B finishes 7 of 10 tasks but has no state errors and no failed recoveries.
Its score is 0.7, so it ranks higher because it handles personal context more reliably.

math.note: The benchmark reports richer metrics than this sketch, but the core idea is to value correct completion only when the agent respects personal state and recovers from mistakes.

charts.title: Performance on generic public-tool benchmarks
charts.note: Strong public-tool results do not imply strong personal-tool results because the personal setting introduces hidden state and permissions.

charts.title: Performance on MCP-Persona
charts.note: The paper reports that current agents struggle because personalized workflows require more careful context use than generic benchmarks demand.

items.b: Simulation may still simplify real personal environments.
items.html: If the simulated apps omit messy edge cases, the benchmark may understate deployment difficulty because real user environments contain more irregular state and more surprising side effects.

items.b: Agents may overfit the benchmark tasks.
items.html: If the task set is narrow, an agent can learn benchmark-specific habits because repeated patterns reduce the need for general personal-state reasoning.

items.b: Single-number reporting can hide failure types.
items.html: If users look only at overall completion, they may miss whether errors came from bad permission handling or bad state reading, because those failure sources need different fixes.

The benchmark is most useful when it preserves detailed personal state and reports detailed failure categories, because developers then learn exactly which part of personal tool use is blocking reliable deployment.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small simulated environment for two or three personal applications such as messaging, social posting, and document sharing. Give each test user different histories and permissions. Run several agents on the same tasks and log whether they inspect user state before acting, whether they choose the correct tool path, and whether they recover after a wrong action.
The demo should show that public-tool competence does not carry over automatically to personal tools, because the benchmark's value comes from exposing account-specific failure modes.
demo.closing: A convincing demo must show that personal state changes the correct workflow, because without that property the benchmark would collapse back into a generic tool-use test.
